newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Espy aide pleads innocent to criminal charges.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Espy aide pleads innocent to criminal charges.

text.p: The top aide to former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy pleaded innocent Monday to criminal charges of hiding some $22,000 in fees he received from farm groups while working for Espy.

Ronald Blackley, who served as Espy's chief of staff, entered his plea at a brief arraignment in federal district court. District Judge Royce Lamberth denied a request by his lawyers for two months to file various motions in the case, ordering the defence to complete its paperwork within 10 days.

Federal prosecutors said they hoped to take the case to trial by early July. "We'll certainly be ready within the 70-day time period mandated by the speedy trial rule," prosecutor William Fahey said, adding that the trial should be wrapped up in about three days.

Last week, a federal grand jury indicted Blackely on three counts of making false statements to federal investigators and hiding income that was not allowed under government ethics rules. The indictment charges him with failing to report fees he received for helping farmer clients obtain subsidies from the Agriculture Department while he worked there.

Before joining Espy's staff, he ran a consulting business in which he helped producers get federal subsidies from the farm agency. Blackely, who is on administrative leave from his job at the U.S. Agency for International Development, could face up to 15 years in prison and a fine of $750,000 if found guilty of all charges.

The prosecution also said it would seek to have one of Blackley's attorneys dismissed from the case because of an alleged conflict of interest. Jeffrey Jacobovitz, a Washington lawyer, represented Blackley's college-age son during the grand jury investigation, Fahey said.

The son, a student at Mississippi State, testified to the grand jury about his father's receipt of the $22,000 in fees, prosecutors said. Jacobovitz told the court there was no conflict of interest and that Blakeley's son would be called as a defence witness in the case.
Defence lawyers also said they might seek to move the trial out of Washington.

The indictment marked the first criminal charges against a member of Espy's staff in the 30-month investigation of the former Clinton cabinet member. He has been under investigation since late 1994 for allegedly accepting illegal gifts and favours while he was agriculture secretary from companies his agency regulated.
